title: What Breaks When You Build AI Under Sovereignty Constraints - Bilge Yücel, deepset GmbH
talk_summary: A vendor talk from deepset about 'sovereignty' (data/model/infrastructure/operational control) framed for regulated enterprises, with Haystack as the recommended orchestration layer. The transferable engineering content is thin: model swappability, typed/explicit data flow, YAML-serialized pipelines for versioning, and dynamic tool search to avoid stuffing tool definitions into context.

takeaways.what_they_do: They argue systems should let you change model providers without rewriting application logic, and treat tight coupling to one provider as a risk (outage, price hike).
takeaways.evidence_quote: if your system can only work with one specific model, you are tightly coupled with that model provider

takeaways.technique: Dynamic tool search instead of full tool schemas in context
takeaways.what_they_do: When an agent has hundreds of tools, they index tool definitions in a searchable tool set (BM25) and retrieve only relevant ones rather than putting all definitions in the prompt.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you probably now have more than hundreds of tools to for your agent, but you don't want to fill in the whole context with just tool definitions

takeaways.technique: Typed, explicit data flow and traceable tool calls
takeaways.what_they_do: Every component input/output is typed and declared, and in agent architectures tool calls and tool outputs are traceable spans, so you can read the pipeline definition and know what data went where.
takeaways.evidence_quote: every input and output in a Haystack application is typed and declared

takeaways.technique: Serialize pipeline/agent config to version-controlled YAML
takeaways.what_they_do: Applications are serializable to YAML so the whole pipeline definition can be committed and rolled back to a prior commit/hash.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the Haystack applications are serializable to YAML making them very easy to version

takeaways.technique: Input/output guardrail components around the agent
takeaways.what_they_do: They place a guardrail before the agent (prompt-injection/regulatory check, unsafe input exits early) and a compliance guardrail after it before returning output.
takeaways.evidence_quote: there is the last guardrail doing a compliance checks because you also don't want to leak sensitive information to your user

takeaways.what_they_do: They define per-tool confirmation policies: some actions always require human approval, others ask once then run freely within the cycle.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if the agent wants to use the list payment request tool, maybe ask for a permission first from the human
